touches.text: Librarian: the embedding links work better without device boundaries in the way (4.5.2).
Inference Ticket: the record of one call to the inference proxy, everything that happened to that request.
Used for learning, or for debugging when something fails. A logging artifact, so transient (4.3.2): disposable after 30 days.
Knowledge: one list of nodes, owned by the librarian.

Ownership. The librarian owns every tree and delegates some to the devices that learn. EVERYTHING THAT LEARNS USING OUR GRAPH TREES IS A DELEGATE (CodeMother, chart and any learning block are examples, not a list), and each holds its trees by the librarian's delegation (Law 6: delegation through the owner's gate). WHY: two holders with different weights over the same nodes have different perspectives and can debate points, and the librarian, asked anything, can look at the query from both.

The memory model. Everything Cairn keeps as LEARNING in database memory is these five things, and only these. Logs, troubles, git records and a device's own state keep their own homes (4.3.2-4.3.4). WHY: one kind of access everywhere.
Nodes: one long list, id = row. Every tree indexes it; no tree owns a node, so several trees can index the same node in different ways.
Trees as tables, permanent: each asks one question, with the weights in its leaves. A tree past 5K leaves is calved at its dominant attractors, a deterministic code shear.

Bidirectional links, in lists of their own, id = row. A link that carries a tree's weights lives in that tree's own link list, because the weights belong to the tree's question. A link that is a fact about two nodes (derived from, part of, contradicts) lives in one shared list, readable from either end.
Blobs (books, pages, screenshots): a file named by its content hash, plus a node that points at it. A remote box that syncs its db (11.3.5.1) syncs its blobs too.

Embeddings. Not every node gets one. WHY: embedding every single thing would make an impossible mound of data, and that is not how Akien works, and this is meant to work the way he does. What gets embedded is the pattern: the answers to a few key questions that cross domains (4.3.1.8). A node without an embedding is found by its key (eg an exact request).

Lifetimes. Each tree declares its lifetime when it is made: kept, one activity (eg one sleep run), or until its source file changes. Dropping a tree drops its leaves and its own links. A node goes only when no tree indexes it, so whatever a temporary tree's activity promoted into a permanent tree outlives it. The drop is enforced, not a habit. WHY: a run that ends without dropping its tables leaves them behind forever.

Cross-domain questions (cognition questions): inherently cross domain, not domain specific. "How might that work?" is Akien's number one: "it's applicable in almost all domains, and captures the pattern, not the domain specific answer." They are not design questions: a design question is a spec choice waiting on Akien (cairn question, CairnCommons/questions/).

A question is a node in the one list. Two devices can have the same question: both hold the same node. Owning a question = holding a tree for it, with that device's own weights, as the librarian's delegate (4.3.1.4).
Transient: things held for seconds to days (mail, logs, test runs, trouble tickets, inference tickets). The logging tree.

What Cairn stores in the database is a tree, with few exceptions (4.3.1.5). Transient trees are the mechanism for a transient need that wants one: like a temp folder, there are many, each made when it is needed and tossed when it is done. Nothing transient MUST be in a tree.

Transient things may help debugging out to 30 days and won't be needed past that, eg an inference ticket looked at a week later because a bug turned up. No trouble should stand unresolved at 30 days; sleep's cleanup may be made to spare one that does.
Shareable provenance (charters, tickets, validations) is git JSON beside the code, never a row.
Holds the metrics table (17.27) until Recovery exists (6.6.3.4). Akien 2026-11-09: "the cairn device holds it until recovery exists".
It owns all system metrics: the metrics table (17.27). Until Recovery exists the cairn device holds it (5.3.6).
Owns the graph trees: the one list of nodes, and each depositor's index over them (4.3.1.1). Owns all learning in the system and delegates it (4.3.1.4); CC's learning records belong here too.
TOOLS: trees (its own, published as a client tool); base, question, bus_client, system_word, gate; machines learning_block, web_operator; db client.

Who holds tables: every table of learning is a tree in the memory model (4.3.1.5), owned by the librarian and delegated to the devices that learn. A table that is not learning is an exception and names why; the bus's message table is the first (5.5.3.4.1).
INFERENCE PROXY DEVICE (cairn/devices/inferenceproxy/)
A request seen before is answered from the stored answer, if it still holds, and the host is not touched. That untouched call is compilation.

The stored answers are learning, so they live in the memory model: a tree the proxy holds by the librarian's delegation, asking "what did this request answer?". An answer is found by its exact request and carries no embedding (4.3.1.6). The meter (every call, its verdict and cost) is not learning: it is metrics (17.27). The inference ticket, a file in the logs tree on the 30 day clock, is only for debugging.

The yield report (tokens spent against tokens saved, the meter for Telos 1) reads the metrics table (17.27): each call records its spent, saved and latency rows under the call as subject, kept forever, so the all-time total is a sum. Akien 2026-11-09, answering Q#78: "inference tickets are only for debugging, so we can't use that as a metric."

Machine: route, the sieves (enabled, never_routed, serves_kind, keyed, addressed) built with the nest machine (16.2), cheapest survivor first. Nests are how the inference proxy resolves its routing questions.
VERBS: infer, embed, resolve, calls. COMMANDS: cairn inference show.

metric: records a measurement of anything. WHY: a metric is a primitive; its job is to measure whatever it is, and like feedback (which a metric strictly is) it must eventually have a consumer. USERS: any probe or tool.
A metric is recorded into its holder's data recorder (17.7): no bus, no database. A probe that records and does not send is recording metrics.

Metrics land in one table so any metric can be reported fast from one place: at, name, source (the device/tool that recorded it), start, end, value, unit, subject (the thing measured), info (json). Fields not relevant to a source stay blank. Indexed on name and source by time. One thing (eg an inference call) may record several metrics in its short life, sharing one subject.
Each metric name is declared, with its consumer, in the charter of the component that records it. A name with no consumer is a red.
